claims.text: The target material family is multiphase refractory high-entropy alloys.
The primary mechanical property of interest is tensile ductility.
Multiphase RHEAs will undergo a ductile-brittle-ductile transition during aging at 400–700 °C.
The non-monotonic ductility transition is driven by chemical ordering followed by phase decomposition and re-stabilization of a disordered matrix.
Solutionized WTaMoNbV or CoCrFeNiTi contains a mixture of disordered BCC and FCC solid solutions.
The initial multiphase alloy has no long-range chemical ordering.
Aging at 400–700 °C can induce chemical ordering and phase evolution in the proposed alloys without melting or complete decomposition.
Aging produces ordered B2 or L12 precipitates that subsequently dissolve.
The initially formed ordered precipitates impede dislocation motion and cause an intermediate brittle state.
Coarsening or decomposition of the ordered phases restores dislocation mobility and ductility at longer aging times.
Short-range chemical ordering at low aging times increases the Peierls stress.
Short-range chemical ordering at low aging times reduces stacking-fault energy.
A reduced Peierls barrier at longer aging times enables dislocation cross-slip and twinning.
Ductility versus aging time will follow a U-shaped curve, initially decreasing and then recovering.
Conventional single-principal-element alloys or simple solid solutions typically show a monotonic loss of ductility during aging.
The transition requires atomic-size mismatch and valence-electron concentration values that favor metastable ordered phases.
The Cantor alloy is generally a chemically disordered FCC solid solution below its solidus.
The proposed ductile-brittle-ductile transition is not expected in single-phase FCC alloys such as the Cantor alloy.
The transition is not expected when ordering causes immediate catastrophic phase separation.
Supporting the hypothesis requires showing that B2 or L12 ordering precedes the brittle regime and that its coarsening, dissolution, or decomposition precedes ductility recovery.
